3. On 6-6-2008 the petitioner as plaintiff No.2 conjointly with plaintiff  No.1 filed the Title Suit No.2447 of 2008 for confirmation of possession, realization of money and for permanent as well as mandatory injunction impleading opposite party Nos. 1-7 as defendants in the court of learned 3rdJoint District Judge, Dhaka. Thereafter, on 20-5-2009 the plaintiff No.1 filed an application under Order XXIII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure (hereinafter referred to as the CPC) for striking out his name from the plaint which was allowed on 22-1-2012 by Order No.51. Then, on 22-3-20 12 the plaintiff No, 2, the present-petitioner, filed an application before the trial court for adding the former plaintiff No.1 as defendant No.8 in the suit invoking Order I, rule 10(2) read with section 151 of the CPC but the same was rejected by the learned 3rri Joint District Judge Court, Dhaka on 23-7-2012 against which the present-petitioner moved before this Court. Hence, this Rule. 

 7. Per contra, Mr Aktar Imam, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No.7, at the very outset of making his submissions, takes us through the averments of the plaint and canvasses that the plaint itself is liable to be rejected under Order VII, rule 11 of the CPC in that the suit is clearly barred by law. In an endeavour to elaborate the said point of argument, he places the relevant provisions of law namely, sections 17 A and 17B of the Registration Act, 1908 and submits that there is a mandatory requirement of law to get a contract registered within 30 days from the date of entering into a land-related agreement and in the present suit the contract being an unregistered one the suit fails on the face of the averments of the plaint. Thereafter, he places section 21A of the SR Act, 1877 and submits that there are 2 mandatory components of this provision of law namely, the contract must be a written registered instrument and the balance amount of consideration must be deposited in the court at the time of filing the suit for specific performance of contract, however, the plaintiff-petitioner in order to circumvent the requirements of the said provisions of law opted not to institute a suit for specific performance of contract and instead filed the suit in the present form. He submits that a plaint may be rejected at any phase, even at the fag end of the hearing of a suit, and although it has been lately surfaced that the plaint is liable to be rejected under the provisions of Order VII, rule 11 (d) of the CPC as the suit is barred by the provisions of sections 17 A and 17B of the Registration Act, 1908 as well as section 21A of the SR Act, this Court is well empowered to reject the plaint without wasting further time by letting this suit proceed further by the trial court. As per Mr. Aktar Imam allowing the present application for addition of party will merely waste the valuable time of the trial court in view of the fact that ultimately the suit itself will fail on the law points as raised by him. In support of the submissions advanced by the learned Advocate for opposite party No.7 the following case laws were referred to namely, Burmah Eastern Ltd vs Burmah Eastern Employees Union, 18 DLR 709, Abdul Jalil vs Islami Bank Bangladesh Ltd, 53 DLR (AD) 12 and Rasheda Begum vs Nurussafa, 2004 BLD (AD) 223 = 9 BLC (AD) 223. 

 9. We have heard the learned Advocates for the petitioner, opposite party Nos. 5-6 and opposite party No.7, perused the application under section 115 of the CPC together with the impugned order and the annexures appended thereto and we have also minutely considered the decisions and relevant laws placed before this Court. 

 12. Now, let us deal with the issue of rejection of plaint under Order VII, rule 11 read with section 151 of the CPC as raised by Mr Akter Imam. From the averment of the plaint it appears that there was an agreement between the plaintiff and defendant Nos. 2-3 and it is the case of the plaintiff that out of the total agreed amount of Taka 33,00,000 (Thirty three lakh) already an amount of Taka 32,50,000 (Thirty two lakh and fifty thousand) has been paid by the former to the latter pursuant to the said agreement and it has been claimed by the plaintiff that as she has been in possession of the suit land since 1985, she has acquired a legal right thereto. However, since the claim as to the possession of the plaintiff has been denied by defendants, the same appears to us to be a disputed question of fact which requires adjudication through evidence. Thus, the claim of the plaintiff as to making payment of the said amount of money as well as to have the possession in the suit plot shows that there is a cause of action and the suit, therefore, may proceed towards its final disposal. Regarding the argument that the suit is barred by law, in our way of scrutiny, we find that the suit is not barred by the provisions of Registration Act or SR Act given that the plaintiff has not sought for performance of the said contract. 

 13.Secondly, our consistent view as to the provisions of Order VII, rule 11 is that the Legislature has incorporated the said provision to save the time of the Courts as well as the bonafide litigants. Since a plaint containing the defects, which are encapsulated in (a) to (d) of rule 11 under Order VII, is liable to be rejected, the defect should be spotted by the Courts or the parties to the suit at the earliest possible phase of the suit. It is to be borne in mind that the Legislature did not contemplate that the provisions of rejection of the plaint they 'inscribed in the CPC would be frequently and indiscriminately used for dismissal of the suits inasmuch as the Legislature purposefully used the words 'plaint', thus, not ‘suit’, and 'rejection', in contrast with the perception of 'dismissal' as the Part/Chapter of the ere in which they have chosen to incorporate the said provision is under the heading of ‘PLAINT’, a provision which primarily deals with the ins and outs of a plaint in a suit. Also, following the rejection of plaint, since Order VII, rule 13 allows for the. Presentation of a fresh plaint in respect of the same cause of action, it distinguishes the consequence of the rejection of a plaint from the dis- missal of a suit. The reason behind ushering the above discussion is that bulks of the learned Advocates perceive the provision of rejection of plaint to be the final ending of a suit. They should not make the application using the word 'rejection rather they should employ the worlds ‘application for dismissal of the suit' if that is what they intend and, of course, they should not invoke the provisions under Order VII, rule 11 of the CPC. In these days, we very often notice that the learned Advocates tend to invoke the provisions of Order VII, rule 11 simply to protract the disposal of the suit. In view of the fact that it has been 7 years since institution of the suit and the parties of the suit could have adjudicated upon the suit by adducing evidence within this time but instead of assisting the learned trial court in adjudication upon the suit, the mere attempt of approaching by defendant No.7 seeking rejection of the plaint at this stage does not appear to be a bonafide step. This Court has discouraged the above kind of move in a number of judgments passed by it In the recent past. In the case of Salauddin vs MA Hai 63 DLR (AD) 138, when the suit was at the stage of peremptory hearing and the defendant filed application for rejection of the plaint under section 151 of the CPC after 9 years, the Apex Court disapproved the said move by the defendant. 

 14. We, thus, opine that since the suit was filed on 6-6-2008 and its peremptory hearing is awaiting, at this juncture, after such a long period defendants should put their best endeavour to dispose of the suit through full trial instead of attempting to get the plaint rejected only. Since the provisions of rejection of the plaint have been incorporated in the CPC for the purpose of convenience of the bonafide litigants so as to, allow them to find the appropriate forum or to mention the right cause of action in the fresh plaint as soon as the defect is surfaced, the present move by defendant No.7 seeking the rejection of plaint after such a long period of 7 years does not appear to be compatible with the scheme of provisions of Order VII, rule 11 of the CPC. However, where the provisions of Order VII, rule 11 of the CPC do not strictly fit in but in the opinion of the courts there is a clear and unambiguous case of res sub-judice, res judicata or an out and out false case upon tallying the identities. of the parties to the suit, comparing the subject matter of the suit and scanning the cause of action of the suits and, further, there is no new or further issue to be adjudicated upon, in that rare event, the courts may reject the, plaint even at a belated stage, having exercised-their inherent powers under section 151of the CPC.
